longevity.headline: Physical Activity Linked to Delayed Ovarian Aging via Adiponectin Signaling
longevity.summary: A mixed-methods study combined observational data from 152,435 UK Biobank participants with mechanistic mouse models to examine how exercise influences reproductive longevity. In the human cohort, higher physical activity was associated with delayed markers of ovarian aging, while mouse experiments indicated that exercise preserved ovarian function and extended reproductive lifespan through adiponectin-related pathways. While the rodent findings demonstrated a causal mechanism via adiponectin, the human data remain observational and cannot establish direct causation. The primary limitation is that mechanistic longevity outcomes in rodents do not directly translate to clinical reproductive timing in humans. Because the full abstract was unavailable at the time of review, this summary is based on publication details and discussion. Practical meaning: Regular physical activity supports general metabolic health, but whether it directly extends human reproductive lifespan remains under investigation.

primaryLinks.title: Physical activity delays ovarian aging in part through adiponectin-related signaling pathways

longevity.headline: Lower Plasma Selenium Linked to Higher All-Cause and Cancer Mortality in Older Adults
longevity.summary: In a 9-year prospective cohort study of 1,389 older French adults (aged ~60–71 at baseline), researchers examined the relationship between baseline plasma selenium levels and mortality. Over the follow-up period, 101 participants died. Those who died had significantly lower baseline plasma selenium levels compared to survivors (mean 1.01 vs. 1.10 µmol/L). After adjusting for sociodemographic, dietary, cognitive, and health factors, each 0.2 µmol/L decrease in plasma selenium was associated with a 54% higher risk of all-cause mortality (adjusted RR 1.54, 95% CI 1.25–1.88) and a 79% higher risk of cancer mortality (adjusted RR 1.79, 95% CI 1.32–2.44). As an observational study, these results show an association rather than direct causation; lower selenium may reflect baseline subclinical illness, frailty, or overall poorer nutritional status. Practical meaning: Maintaining adequate dietary intake of essential trace minerals like selenium supports general health, but observational associations do not justify taking unguided high-dose supplements.

primaryLinks.title: Selenium and mortality in the elderly: results from the EVA study.

longevity.headline: Scientific Debate Continues Over Sirtuins and the Information Theory of Aging
longevity.summary: Because an abstract was unavailable, this summary is based on the linked scientific discussion regarding a published analysis of sirtuins and conceptual models of aging. The piece represents a critical academic evaluation questioning the evidentiary foundation behind sirtuin-targeted longevity claims and whether the 'information theory of aging' has been rigorously tested. A key limitation is that this discussion centers on basic biochemical theory and preclinical models rather than direct human clinical trial outcomes. Practical meaning: High-profile biological theories of aging remain subject to active debate among researchers and are not yet established guides for human longevity interventions.

primaryLinks.title: Life Metabolism Analysis on Sirtuins and Aging Models

longevity.headline: Midlife blood metabolites, including ergothioneine, linked to brain health and cognition
longevity.summary: In an observational cohort study of 1,082 dementia-free middle-aged adults from the Rotterdam Study (replicated in two independent cohorts), researchers evaluated 991 blood metabolites against brain MRI metrics and cognitive function. Fourteen metabolites showed replicated associations with cognitive performance, with the dietary antioxidant ergothioneine demonstrating the strongest positive link. Environmental and clinical factors—such as diet, gut microbiome, and medications—explained up to 28.6% of metabolite variance, substantially exceeding genetic contributions. Notably, antacid use was linked to lower ergothioneine levels, statistically mediating 31.5% of the association between antacid use and lower cognitive scores. Because this is an observational study, these correlations do not establish causation or prove that ergothioneine supplementation prevents dementia. Practical meaning: Blood metabolites provide valuable research insights into how lifestyle, gut health, and medications interact with brain aging, but they are not yet actionable screening tools or validated targets for self-directed supplementation.

primaryLinks.title: The blood metabolome of brain health in midlife and influences of genes, microbiome and exposome

longevity.headline: Metabolically Healthy Obesity Linked to Increased Cardiovascular and Mortality Risk
longevity.summary: In a prospective cohort study of 157,159 UK Biobank adults followed for a median of 12.9 years, researchers examined whether obesity without baseline metabolic abnormalities (hypertension, diabetes, or dyslipidemia) is truly benign. Compared with normal-weight individuals free of metabolic abnormalities, men with 'metabolically healthy' obesity had a higher relative risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (HR 1.46), heart failure (HR 1.63), steatotic liver disease (HR 2.37), and all-cause mortality (HR 1.36). Similar elevations were observed in women (heart failure HR 1.69; all-cause mortality HR 1.27). When metabolic abnormalities were present, risks rose substantially higher. Because this was an observational study with baseline exposure measurements, it cannot establish direct causality or account for metabolic changes over time. Practical meaning: Having normal blood pressure, lipids, and glucose does not completely offset the long-term health risks associated with obesity, supporting discussions with a clinician on comprehensive weight and metabolic management.

primaryLinks.title: Obesity, metabolic health status, and adverse outcomes in men and women.

longevity.headline: Menopausal Estrogen Therapy Linked to Lower Alzheimer's Neuropathology in Cohort Study
longevity.summary: In an observational autopsy study of two US cohorts (reported here based on the linked discussion, as the full abstract was unavailable), women who used menopausal estrogen therapy had roughly 35% lower odds of Alzheimer's disease neuropathology at death alongside fewer clinical dementia diagnoses. Because this study is observational, it identifies an association rather than proving causation, and findings may be influenced by confounding factors such as the healthy user effect. Practical meaning: These findings add to ongoing research on hormone therapy and brain health, but decisions about starting or continuing menopausal hormone therapy should be made with your clinician based on individualized symptom management and overall risk profile.

primaryLinks.title: Association Between Menopausal Hormone Therapy and Alzheimer Disease Neuropathology

longevity.headline: Observational Study Examines Physical Fitness and Mortality in Older Adults
longevity.summary: Based on the linked discussion of a study published in JAMA Network Open, researchers evaluated the association between measured physical fitness levels and all-cause mortality among older adults. Detailed cohort numbers, specific interventions, and quantitative effect sizes were not provided in the discussion. Because this report reflects observational data, it indicates an association rather than direct causation, with baseline comorbidities and reverse causation serving as key potential limitations. Practical meaning: Maintaining routine physical activity and functional fitness into older age remains a low-risk, broadly supported cornerstone of long-term health.

primaryLinks.title: Physical Fitness and All-Cause Mortality in Older Adults

longevity.headline: Plant Fat Intake Linked to Lower Overall and Cardiovascular Mortality in Large Cohort
longevity.summary: In a prospective cohort study analyzing 407,531 US adults (NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study, mean age 61) over 24 years of follow-up, researchers evaluated the relationship between specific dietary fat sources and mortality. Comparing the highest to lowest intake quintiles, higher plant fat consumption—particularly from vegetable oils and grains—was associated with lower overall mortality (adjusted absolute risk difference [ARD] -1.10%; hazard ratio [HR] 0.91) and cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality (adjusted ARD -0.73%; HR 0.86). In contrast, higher intake of animal fat was associated with increased overall mortality (adjusted ARD +0.78%; HR 1.16) and CVD mortality (adjusted ARD +0.32%; HR 1.14). Statistically substituting 5% of energy from animal fat with plant fat was associated with a 4% to 24% lower risk of total mortality. As an observational study, these results show association rather than direct causation, and a major limitation is the reliance on self-reported dietary intake measured only at baseline. Practical meaning: Swapping some dietary animal fats for plant-based sources like vegetable oils and whole grains is a low-risk dietary shift associated with modest long-term survival benefits.

primaryLinks.title: Plant and Animal Fat Intake and Overall and Cardiovascular Disease Mortality.

longevity.headline: JAMA Article Highlights the Role of Sleep Health in Obesity Prevention and Treatment
longevity.summary: A publication in JAMA co-authored by UC San Diego sleep medicine faculty examines how sleep health directly influences obesity prevention and clinical management. Because the full study text and abstract were unavailable at the time of writing, this account is based on the linked announcement. While extensive observational and experimental evidence connects poor sleep duration and quality to altered metabolic hormones and increased weight gain, specific effect sizes, study design, and patient demographics cannot be confirmed from the post alone. The primary limitation is the absence of detailed trial data in the available summary. Practical meaning: Maintaining consistent, restorative sleep serves as a supportive, low-risk foundation alongside nutrition and physical activity for metabolic health.

primaryLinks.title: JAMA: Sleep Health and Obesity Prevention and Treatment

longevity.headline: US Excess Mortality Linked to Cardiometabolic Disease, Substance Use, and Suicide
longevity.summary: Based on the linked discussion of a JAMA Network Open study comparing United States mortality data against other high-income nations, the widening gap in US excess deaths is largely driven by surges in circulatory and metabolic disorders, drug overdoses, alcohol-induced mortality, and suicide. Because full abstract details and effect sizes were unavailable, this summary relies on reported excerpts. As a population-level observational analysis, the findings capture broad epidemiological trends rather than individual-level causal mechanisms. Practical meaning: Broad-based preventive care addressing foundational cardiometabolic health and substance or mental health support represents a primary target for mitigating premature mortality risk.

primaryLinks.title: Causes of Excess Deaths in the US Compared With Other High-Income Countries

longevity.headline: Evening Light-Emitting eReader Use Delays Melatonin Release and Impairs Sleep Quality
longevity.summary: In a controlled crossover laboratory study, healthy adults read either a light-emitting eReader or a printed book for four hours before bedtime across five consecutive evenings. Compared to print reading, backlit screen exposure significantly suppressed evening melatonin secretion, prolonged sleep latency, delayed the circadian clock by over an hour, reduced REM sleep, and diminished next-morning alertness. Because this was a controlled inpatient trial, causal effects of evening screen light are established, though the primary limitation is that strict laboratory lighting conditions may overestimate or differ from variable home environments and modern device night modes. Practical meaning: Switching from backlit electronic screens to printed materials in the hours before bed helps protect natural melatonin production, shorten time to fall asleep, and improve morning alertness.

primaryLinks.title: Evening use of light-emitting eReaders negatively affects sleep, circadian timing, and next-morning alertness

longevity.headline: Review Explores Yogurt's Role in Cardiometabolic Health and Healthy Aging
longevity.summary: This narrative review traces the history and scientific evidence surrounding yogurt consumption and aging-related chronic conditions, particularly cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. The authors highlight that yogurt's combination of lactic acid bacteria, probiotics, and bioactive nutrients may beneficially influence gut microbiota-derived metabolites linked to cardiometabolic risk. However, the paper emphasizes that many underlying biological mechanisms and direct therapeutic thresholds remain unproven, and observational associations may be confounded by overall diet quality and lifestyle factors. Practical meaning: Incorporating unsweetened fermented dairy like yogurt can fit into a healthy, balanced diet, though specific longevity or therapeutic benefits are still being actively investigated.

primaryLinks.title: Yogurt and human health across history, culture, and science: Lessons for modern aging populations.
